blocks.text: Holding the Name at the Moment of Death

inline.s: Only keep the four characters Amitabha Buddha in mind and never forget them. If you are able to recite aloud, recite aloud; if you can only recite softly, recite softly. And if you can do neither, then hold the four characters silently in your heart and let them never be lost. Those who attend you at the bedside should likewise constantly remind you of these four characters. Know that all the stray paths you have wandered through a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives are cut off cleanly in this very moment, by a single thought. Why is this so? The wheel of the six realms is governed by one thought as master. If that thought is fixed entirely upon the Buddha, then though the body decays, the spirit does not scatter, and following that single thought one is reborn in the Pure Land. Alas! Only keep the four characters Amitabha Buddha in mind, and never forget them.

blocks.text: Making Vows, Confessing, and Reciting the Name

inline.s: Alas! How many people in this world fail to understand the recitation of the Buddha's name! The Confucians cast Buddhism aside as heterodox and refuse to recite; monastics make of the recitation a set routine and do not know why they recite; those of wild wisdom know there is a Buddha yet disdain to recite; the foolish and deluded do not know the Buddha and so are unable to recite. This is the general picture
(speaking broadly)

, and even among village men and women, who upon hearing of cause and effect do come to know the recitation and practice it, they yet hanker after blessings in a life to come and so remain seeds of the wheel of rebirth. Of those who seek one that recites in order to transcend birth and death, there are barely one or two in a hundred. Know that once a person recites the Buddha's name, he should take up the Buddha's compassionate heart, practice the Buddha's compassionate deeds, make vast vows, and deliver sentient beings; for all defilements and karmic entanglements he should universally repent; and every merit, great and small, he should dedicate toward the Western Land. Only this is the true cause of reciting the Buddha's name.

blocks.text: Appendix: A Plain Explanation of the Ten Transcendent Benefits of Reciting the Buddha's Name in This Present Life

inline.s: Explained by the Venerable Elder Master Changzhen

A single recitation of the Buddha's name is the crystallization of ten thousand kinds of merit, possessing an inconceivable, mighty spiritual power. It is the compassionate ferry across the sea of birth and death, the bright lamp in the endless night. Especially for the sentient beings of the Latter Age of the Dharma, whose faculties are inferior and who face many conditions for backsliding. As the Great Jewel Heap Sutra says: "In the Latter Age, among untold millions upon millions who cultivate, scarce one attains the Way (realizes the fruit of the path); only by relying on the recitation of the Buddha's name are they able to transcend birth and death." The modern eminent monk Master Daoyuan likewise said: "For the sentient beings of the Latter Age, there is no way to end birth and death save by reciting the Buddha's name, and no way to deliver sentient beings save by reciting the Buddha's name." (Master Daoyuan: Lectures on the Amitabha Sutra.) This shows that the practice of reciting the Buddha's name is the sovereign remedy for the sentient beings of the Latter Age.

Some people suppose that the practice of reciting the Buddha's name is meant for the elderly — a way of idling away their days and awaiting death, useful only at the last hour. These are all one-sided and mistaken views. In truth, our own mind is the Buddha; to recite the Buddha's name is to recite the mind — this is what is meant by "the mind is what makes the Buddha." "Cast the Buddha's name into a confused mind, and the confused mind cannot but become the Buddha (the Buddha-mind)." Layman Xia Lianju put it well: "Recite Amitabha, recite on straight ahead — it turns out that it is Amitabha reciting Amitabha." From this it is clear that a single name-recitation can release one from birth and death, escape the wheel of rebirth, be reborn in the Pure Land, and perfectly realize bodhi — truly the shortest cut within the shortest cut. One further point must be made clear: recitation does not only bring great benefit at the moment of death; it brings great benefit even in this present life. Master Yinguang said: all things can be accomplished by reciting the Buddha's name to seek their fulfillment — except doing evil.

The ten kinds of transcendent benefit gained in this present life through reciting the Buddha's name, as set forth in this article, form a fairly comprehensive summing up. These were all spoken personally by the Buddha and were excerpted from the Buddhist scriptures. The Buddha never speaks falsely — do not doubt them in the least! For the convenience of beginners, I have made this humble and plain explanation. If there is anything inappropriate, I respectfully beg your correction.
1. One constantly enjoys the invisible protection of all heavenly gods.

All the heavenly gods within the celestial realms revere the Buddha Dharma. The merit of our recitation is certain to move the gods, who rejoice, praise it, and protect us in unseen ways. Therefore, the person who recites, without praying for the dispelling of calamities and the averting of misfortune, naturally has calamities dispelled and misfortune averted; without praying for his family's peace, his family is naturally at peace. For the reciter this is but a small benefit gained in this present life. For the gods, too, it is the accumulation of merit, so that both sides are benefited.
2. One constantly enjoys the ever-present protection and following of all bodhisattvas.

The task of the bodhisattvas is, above, to seek the Buddha Way, and, below, to transform sentient beings. For this reason they constantly manifest immeasurable bodies, roaming the ten directions to deliver those who are bound by conditions. The sentient beings who recite the Buddha's name are bound by conditions to the buddhas and bodhisattvas; when beings in the sea of birth and death single-mindedly call out the name, they are sending a cry for help to the buddhas and bodhisattvas. Hence the ancient worthy said: "In the sea of birth and death, to recite the Buddha's name comes first." Calling the name for rescue is the cause; the bodhisattva, hearing the sound and saving from suffering, is the condition. When cause and condition meet and the spiritual response is joined, then misfortune turns to fortune and suffering gives way to joy — this is the fruit. Through the ages many bound sentient beings, having called on the name amid disasters and distress, have turned peril into safety through that calling; and having gained the benefits of recitation, they have given rise to faith and made vows, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma. "First entice them with what they desire, then lead them into the Buddha's wisdom" — this is the skillful means by which the bodhisattvas transform and deliver sentient beings.
3. One constantly enjoys the day-and-night protection and remembrance of all buddhas, and Amitabha Buddha constantly radiates light to gather in and receive this person.

Constantly protected and remembered by all buddhas: to protect means to guard; to remember means to bear in mind. The Amitabha Sutra says: "These good men and good women are all protected and kept in mind by all the buddhas, and every one of them attains non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment)." This shows that the person who recites the Buddha's name is protected and kept in mind by all the buddhas. Because the power of the buddhas' protection and remembrance is inconceivable, the mind of their cultivation can never retrogress, until they attain the Buddha's wisdom — anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. According to this, even if in this life one cannot be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, still, having already planted the roots of goodness, one will never retrogress, and there will surely come a day when one is reborn in the Pure Land, sees the Buddha, and hears the Dharma.

Amitabha Buddha radiates light to gather in and receive: Amitabha Buddha is also called the Buddha of Boundless Light. The Buddha's light of wisdom pervades the ten directions, transcending space. The Buddha's radiance is a thousand million times greater than the light of the sun; the sun's light is cut off by a single wall. The Buddha's radiance shines on all things, and nothing whatsoever can block it. "Amitabha" means Boundless Light and Boundless Life, and is the Dharmakāya of the Buddha — that is to say, the Buddha-nature inherent in every person. For the reciter, karmic hindrances are dissolved and body and mind become pure; when the mind is pure, the mind is the Buddha. This is the principle of "when falsehood departs, the true is revealed."
4. The person who recites the Buddha's name is illumined all about his body to a distance of forty li; no evil ghosts can harm him, and no snakes, dragons, or poisons can affect him at all.

The everlasting true mind with which every person is endowed is like a great round mirror that mirrors heaven and earth, possessing boundless light. But veiled by the dust of many lives, it grows dim and colorless. A single recitation of the Buddha's name is a purifying agent that dispels false thoughts; when false thoughts are dispelled, the mind's radiance is revealed, and the body emits a light that reaches forty li away. This is real and not false. The Collected Works of Master Ouyi records: In Tongcheng County, Anhui, there were two men, Jia and Yi, who went out to trade; in time Jia fell ill and died in a foreign land. Yi buried him and brought back his belongings, giving them to Jia's wife. As her husband was young and strong, she wondered how he could have died so suddenly, and suspected Yi of murdering him for his wealth. Yi felt deeply wronged, yet had no way to prove his innocence. He went to Jia's grave and wept, pouring out his grievance. Suddenly Jia's voice came close to his ear, saying: "You have been kind to me, and my wife has wronged you. I can cling to your body and return home to explain it to her clearly." So Yi turned back. Along the way Jia conversed with him, just as in life, though only the voice was heard — no form was seen. Once, Yi stumbled by accident and nearly fell. Without thinking, he recited, "Amitabha Buddha!" At that, Jia said in an alarmed voice from afar: "Why do you cast a light and frighten me?" Hearing that recitation emits light, Yi recited the Buddha's name several times more. Then Jia's voice moved still farther away, saying: "When you recite the Buddha's name, your chest radiates a dazzling light, and I cannot come near you. Please go back and tell my wife to come to the grave, and I will explain it to her clearly." Yi did as he was told. Through this, Yi came to feel deeply the inconceivable power of the Buddha, so he gave up commerce, left home to become a monk, and cultivated with undivided devotion. In time he became a great monk.
Again, in the year

, Layman Yang Changping of Chengdu, passing East Gate Bridge one day, stepped on a stone and nearly fell, and without realizing it uttered the recitation "Amitabha Buddha!" That night he had a dream in which five gaily adorned, beautiful women invited him to walk with them. His heart was moved, and he went along with them to a certain street and number; they went in and beckoned to him. At that moment an old man with a white beard blocked his way, saying: "You are a reciter of the Buddha's name — do not go in." He nonetheless pressed on with all his might, and then suddenly awoke. Finding the dream strange, Yang went in person the next day to that street and number and asked the master of the house about the scene of the night before. The host said: "No five beautiful women came. Only, last night my family's mother dog gave birth to
puppies, of which

were female spotted dogs, and one male dog died the moment it was born." Hearing this, Yang broke out in a cold sweat. He thought: had he not uttered a single recitation, he would have gone off and become a dog. From then on he served the Buddha all the more devoutly and often cited this matter to admonish others. The above was personally heard from Yang by Layman Fan Longyi (now
years old, residing at the Recitation and Care Home of Bao Guo Temple in Lezhi).

All demons and spirits fear the light and fear the Buddha's name. The Universal Gateway Chapter says: Suppose in the three thousand great thousand lands there are yakṣas and rākṣasas everywhere, wishing to harm people. When they hear a person call upon the name of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, those evil ghosts dare not even look at him, much less do him harm. Nor will any evil dragons, venomous snakes, or savage beasts harm him. "If savage beasts surround you, with fearful fangs and claws, by the power of thinking on Avalokiteshvara they hasten at once to the boundless regions (fleeing swiftly far away)." "Poisonous serpents and vipers and scorpions, in their venom blazing like smoke and fire, by the power of thinking on Avalokiteshvara, hearing the sound, turn back of their own accord (draw away)." As for poisons, there is also clear instruction: "Curses and all manner of poisons, meant to harm the body, by the power of thinking on Avalokiteshvara, fall back upon the one who sent them (harm-doing harms oneself)." All of the above was spoken personally by the Buddha. Though it speaks of calling upon Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, reciting the Buddha's name is just the same.
5. One is not subject to flood, fire, enemies and thieves, swords and arrows, imprisonment, or death by sudden calamity or wrongful persecution.

The sentient beings of the five turbid ages are beset by all manner of calamities and afflictions without end. Here are listed flood, fire, enmity, bandits, guns and cannon (in ancient times swords and arrows — in our day guns and cannon, all of them weapons that kill; the calamity of sword and arrow also embraces the havoc of war), imprisonment, and death by sudden disaster or wrongful oppression, or a wrongful fall into the evil destinies. In truth, the disasters are far more than these; they are cited merely as representative examples.

The three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion are the root of all evil and the source of every calamity. The person who recites the Buddha's name, in thought after thought, clears away the three poisons and dispels afflictions; without praying for the removal of calamity, he is naturally freed from calamity in the unseen. If in ordinary times he single-mindedly calls on the Buddha's name, then at the critical moment the Amitabha of his own nature will of himself rescue the Amitabha within the minds of sentient beings, and carry him through misfortune to good fortune. If one does not recite in ordinary times, then when disaster befalls, the heart is filled with terror and panic, the faculties are in a whirl, and it is difficult to recall the Buddha's name. Moreover, the secret of reciting the Buddha's name is utmost sincerity and reverence. Master Yinguang said: "With one portion of reverence, one portion of karmic offense is dissolved and one portion of blessing and wisdom is increased; with ten portions of reverence, ten portions of karmic offense are dissolved and ten portions of blessing and wisdom are increased." In this we must hold fast!
6. Karmic actions committed in the past are all wiped away. The wronged lives one has killed are released and delivered, and no longer hold them in thrall.

Since beginningless kalpas we have created karmic evil that is measureless and boundless. If karmic offense had shape and volume, the whole of space could not contain it. Therefore we suffer through long kalpas and are unable to escape. Master Miaokong's Forty-eight Methods of Holding the Name says: "To save one from a moment of suffering, giving is most urgent; to save one from the suffering of ten thousand kalpas, reciting the Buddha's name is most essential." The sutra says, "With a single sincere recitation of the Buddha's name, one can wipe away the heavy sins of birth and death committed over eighty million kalpas." For the wronged lives we have killed in the past, we should earnestly and sincerely call on the Buddha's name to resolve the enmity and untie the knot, so that they may receive the Buddha's compassionate aid and be reborn in a fortunate destiny. Then naturally enmity turns to grace, misfortune to blessing, and the evil retribution of seeking revenge dissolves without a trace.
7. One's dreams by night are upright, or one dreams of the sublime and wondrous bodily form of Amitabha Buddha.

Dreams are manifestations of the mind alone. Those heavy in desire have many lewd and defiled dreams; those heavy in anger have many terrifying dreams. The person who recites the Buddha's name is pure in body and mind, sleeps peacefully at night, and will not have evil or depraved dreams. Moreover, once in bed, silently holding the Buddha's name or quietly listening to a recording of the recitation can nourish the mind and settle the spirit, both counteracting insomnia and dispelling evil dreams. If in a dream one encounters a frightful sight or a nightmare, a single recitation of the Buddha's name instantly turns it into nothing.

Recite the Buddha's name honestly and practice with fine, unbroken effort; false thoughts gradually dissolve, and the mind's radiance gradually appears. When the minds of sentient beings are pure, they see the Buddha; the Buddha at all times and in all places manifests his presence (words of Master Jingkong). When the water is clear, the moon appears of itself — and then one can behold the sublime and majestic wondrous form of Amitabha Buddha. But one must not on that account give rise to a mind of joy or attachment. Far from being beneficial, it will bring harm. Master Yinguang said: "Of late, among those who cultivate, there are many cases of falling under demonic influence. These all come from a restless, reckless mind, eagerly hoping for a spiritual response and for splendid states to appear. You should understand: need it be said that the states which appear are the work of demons? Even a sublime and wondrous state, if a single thought of greedy attachment and delight arises in it, will bring obstacles and harm."
8. One's heart is ever joyful, one's complexion is lustrous and radiant, one's strength is vigorous, and all one does is auspicious.

For the sentient beings of the Saha world, the body is the root of suffering. A lifetime is mostly spent in terror, resentment, sorrow, and pain. Only the person who recites the Buddha's name, with a pure mind, recites single-mindedly, dissolving karma as conditions arise, and is not turned by circumstances. His heart is filled with the joy of Dharma; his countenance is full and radiant, and disease naturally disappears. Health and long life come without being sought — and these are but by-products of the recitation. For the person who recites, all buddhas rejoice, dragons and gods protect, good conditions grow, and whatever he does is necessarily auspicious. Master Jingkong said that in Taiwan there was a male layman, over ninety years of age, who every day walked thirty thousand steps and recited the Buddha's name thirty thousand times; his body was healthy, his spirit full, and his back and spine straight. When the time of his death comes, he will surely be free of all the suffering of illness and pass on in peace.
9. One is ever revered, beloved, and honored by all the people of the world.

The person who recites the Buddha's name is inwardly pure, meets others with harmony, broadly forms good conditions, and finds joy in helping others. Confucius said: "He who respects others is ever respected by them; he who loves others is ever loved by them." (He who respects others plants a good cause, and being ever respected by them reaps a good fruit; he who loves others plants a good cause, and being ever loved by them reaps a good fruit.) Planting such a cause, reaping such a fruit, to be revered, beloved, and honored by people is a matter of necessity.

The nine articles above are all great benefits gained in this present life through reciting the Buddha's name. That view which holds the recitation to be a means of idling away one's days awaiting death, and of use only at the last hour, collapses of itself without needing to be refuted.

10. At the moment of death, one's heart is without fear, right mindfulness is present, and one sees Amitabha Buddha together with the host of sages, who hold a golden lotus to guide and welcome one to rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the West.

Death is the most sorrowful matter in life, and it is one no one can escape. At the moment of death, an emperor of supreme power, a magnate of countless wealth, and a beggar who owns nothing at all are exactly the same. The power and riches in their hands are of no help whatsoever. Only the person who recites the Buddha's name is able at that time to be without attachment and without fear, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. At the same time, he will surely receive the Buddha's guidance to be reborn in the land of the lotus. From then on he transcends the ordinary and enters the holy, until he attains Buddhahood. Of Amitabha Buddha's forty-eight great vows, the nineteenth is the vow of hearing the name and awakening the aspiration, and the twentieth is the vow of receiving and guiding one at the moment of death. The vow reads: "When I attain Buddhahood, may the sentient beings of the ten directions, on hearing my name, awaken the bodhi mind, cultivate all kinds of merit, practice the six pāramitās, firm and never retreating; and, dedicating their roots of goodness, vow to be born in my land, single-mindedly mindful of me day and night without ceasing. At the end of their lives, I, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, shall appear before them. In the space of a moment (in the twinkling of an eye), they shall be born in my Buddha-land (territory) as avivartika (non-retreating) bodhisattvas. Should this vow not be fulfilled, may I not attain perfect enlightenment (if this vow cannot be realized, I vow never to become a Buddha)." This is Amitabha Buddha's guarantee to the sentient beings who recite his name. Is there still any room for doubt?

The ten kinds of benefit above are fully recorded in the scriptures and were proclaimed from the Buddha's golden mouth. Since they bring benefit both in this present life and in the life to come, then of all the essential Dharma-gates within the world and beyond it, there is none more important than reciting the Buddha's name. Only be diligent — do not doubt!

The ten great benefits set forth in this article are all recorded in the Buddhist scriptures and were spoken personally by Śākyamuni Buddha. Since they benefit both the present life and the life to come, then whether viewed from the standpoint of worldly Dharma or of the transcendental Dharma, among all Dharma-gates there is none more important than the practice of reciting the Buddha's name.

But the practice of reciting the Buddha's name is a Dharma-gate that is "easy to practice and hard to believe." Many who study Buddhism do not wholly understand it, and some perhaps still doubt it. As Master Lianchi of the Ming dynasty said in his essay "On Not Being Single-Minded in Recitation" in the Bamboo Window Miscellany: "Formerly, when I was studying at a certain temple, one day the abbot said to the assembly that on the Ghost Festival we should hold a Yulanpen assembly. I supposed we would surely set out a meal and offer it to the community, yet in the end no offering was set out — the abbot merely led the assembly in reciting the Buddha's name for three days. Again, when the head of a certain temple was taken into custody by the authorities, the abbot of the temple gathered the community to perform a Buddhist rite in prayer for his rescue. The assembly thought they would chant sutras and hold mantras, but in the end they only recited the Buddha's name aloud. Both of these matters lay beyond the expectations of ordinary reasoning. One may see that the thoughts and deeds of the great worthies are not commonplace and are well worth learning from. Yet many who recite the Buddha's name today, though they profess single-minded cultivation of the Pure Land, still, in order to prolong their years, chant the Medicine Buddha Sutra; in order to dissolve karmic offenses, bow in the Emperor Liang Repentance; in order to rescue themselves from calamity, recite the disaster-dispelling mantra; in order to seek wisdom, recite the Avalokiteshvara text. They set aside the Buddha-name they ordinarily recite, deeming the recitation of no avail. Why not consider this: Amitabha Buddha is the Buddha of Boundless Life, and those born in his land have life immeasurable as well — how much the more may one beseech a life of a hundred years in the human world? The Contemplation Sutra on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says, "With a single sincere recitation of the Buddha's name, one can wipe away the heavy sins of birth and death committed over eighty million kalpas." How much the more can the calamities before one's very eyes be dispelled? The Larger Sutra of Immeasurable Life says, "I with the light of wisdom broadly illuminate the boundless realms." For the person who recites, Amitabha constantly illumines his body with the light of wisdom — why worry about lacking wisdom? "A single recitation of the Buddha's name is the agada medicine, holding in check all the ten thousand diseases. If you do not believe it and will not take it, of what use is it?" This important instruction, read today, still carries guidance of very pertinent significance.

We who recite the Buddha's name must believe deeply in the Buddha's words. "If the Buddha's words cannot be believed, what words can be believed?" Only be diligent in reciting the Buddha's name, and never doubt in the least! Doubt of itself creates obstacles, and then it will be very hard indeed to obtain the benefits of the recitation.
